hints: Notice what dissolving in a non-polar solvent tells you about bonding, ionic chlorides will not do this but simple covalent ones will.
Steamy fumes that turn moist blue litmus red point to acidic $\text{HCl}$ gas, so M must hydrolyse vigorously in water.
A white precipitate that dissolves in excess $\text{NaOH(aq)}$ to give a colourless solution is the classic test for amphoteric $\text{Al(OH)}_3$, so work back to which cation was in solution R.
walkthrough:
**Use solubility to sort bonding type**

Think like a teacher: like dissolves like. Ionic lattices like $\text{NaCl}$ and $\text{MgCl}_2$ dissolve in polar water but not in non-polar solvents.

A colourless solution in a non-polar solvent means M has covalent character. That fits $\text{AlCl}_3$ and $\text{PCl}_5$, not $\text{NaCl}$ or $\text{MgCl}_2$.

**Interpret the fumes with water**

Adding M to water gives steamy fumes Q that turn moist blue litmus red. That is acidic $\text{HCl}$ gas from vigorous hydrolysis.

Covalent chlorides hydrolyse completely, for example:
$$\text{AlCl}_3 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{Al(OH)}_3 + 3\text{HCl}$$
$$\text{PCl}_5 + 4\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{H}_3\text{PO}_4 + 5\text{HCl}$$

**Use the NaOH test to pick the metal**

Solution R plus a little $\text{NaOH(aq)}$ gives a white precipitate, which dissolves in excess to give a colourless solution. That is exactly amphoteric aluminium hydroxide:
$$\text{Al}^{3+} + 3\text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{Al(OH)}_3 \text{(white ppt)}$$
$$\text{Al(OH)}_3 + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow [\text{Al(OH)}_4]^- \text{(colourless solution)}$$
Phosphorus gives no such precipitate, and magnesium gives a precipitate that does not dissolve. So M must be aluminium chloride.

options.A: Aluminium chloride fits every clue. It has covalent character so dissolves in non-polar solvent, hydrolyses in water to give $\text{HCl}$ steamy fumes, and leaves $\text{Al}^{3+}$ in solution which forms white $\text{Al(OH)}_3$ soluble in excess $\text{NaOH}$ to form $[\text{Al(OH)}_4]^-$.
options.B: Magnesium chloride is ionic. It would not dissolve in a non-polar solvent and it dissolves quietly in water without steamy $\text{HCl}$ fumes. Its white $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ precipitate also does not dissolve in excess $\text{NaOH}$.
options.C: Phosphorus pentachloride is covalent and does hydrolyse to give $\text{HCl}$ fumes, which is a tempting trap. However solution R would contain phosphoric acid, not a metal cation, so it cannot give a white hydroxide precipitate with $\text{NaOH}$.
options.D: Sodium chloride is a typical ionic salt. It is insoluble in non-polar solvent, dissolves in water with no reaction and no fumes, and gives no precipitate at all with $\text{NaOH}$.
